blocks.prompt: The Clock That Started as a Shadow
blocks.text: Look at a clock face. There are twelve numbers on it. The short hand points to the hour. The long hand counts the minutes. The long hand goes all the way around one time every hour. The short hand is so slow that you cannot see it move at all. Long ago, people had no clocks. They watched the sun instead. A stick in the ground made a shadow, and the shadow moved as the sun moved. In the morning the shadow was long. At noon it was short. That was the very first clock. It worked well, but only when the sun was out.

blocks.prompt: The First Clocks Did Not Tick
blocks.text: The first clocks did not tick. They were shadows. In Egypt, more than three thousand years ago, people pushed a stick into the ground and watched its shadow crawl across the dirt. In the morning the shadow was long and pointed one way. By evening it was long again and pointed the other way. At noon it was short. If you carved lines in the ground, you could read the time straight off the shadow. This is also why clock hands turn the way they do. They copy the way a shadow swings. Shadow clocks had one big problem. A cloud stopped them, and night stopped them completely. So people built water clocks. A bowl with a tiny hole let water drip out at a steady rate, and lines inside the bowl showed how much time had gone by. Water clocks worked in the dark. Around seven hundred years ago, towns in Europe put the first big machine clocks in their church towers. Most had no hands and no face at all. They simply rang a bell, so the whole town heard the hour instead of seeing it.

there is no sun at night, so there is no shadow

(inference: everyone could hear it from anywhere, even indoors or in the fields)

4.title: The Clock That Started as a Shadow
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Clock That Started as a Shadow

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A clock is powered by a weight or a spring
The escapement lets the power out tooth by tooth
The tick is the sound of that gate
Galileo studied swinging weights
Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656
Minute hands only became useful after pendulums

blocks.prompt: The Trick Inside the Tick
blocks.text: Every mechanical clock has a hidden problem to solve. A clock is powered by something that badly wants to run: a heavy weight pulling down on a rope, or a coiled spring pushing to unwind. Left alone, that power would spin the gears wildly and dump all of its energy in a few seconds. A clock has to spend that energy slowly and in equal amounts instead. The answer is a part called the escapement. Think of it as a little gate. It blocks the gear train, lets exactly one tooth slip past, then blocks it again. Tooth by tooth, the energy escapes in even portions. That gate opening and closing is the tick you hear. The tick is not decoration. It is the sound of a clock rationing its own power. The escapement still needs something steady to tell it when to open. Early clocks used a swinging bar, which was not steady at all, and they gained or lost a quarter of an hour every day. Then came the pendulum. Galileo noticed something odd about a swinging weight: a wide swing and a small swing take almost exactly the same amount of time. What sets the timing is the length of the string, not the size of the swing. In 1656 a Dutch scientist named Christiaan Huygens used that idea to build the first pendulum clock. Clock error dropped from about fifteen minutes a day to about fifteen seconds a day. Only then was a minute worth measuring, and clocks started growing minute hands.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.
items: What problem does every mechanical clock have to solve?

The passage says minute hands appeared only after pendulum clocks. Why would a minute hand be useless on an older clock?
answers: it has to release stored power slowly and evenly instead of all at once
(it blocks the gears, releases one tooth at a time, then blocks again)
wide and small swings take the same time, and length sets the timing; it gave the escapement something steady to count
(inference: an older clock could be off by fifteen minutes a day, so a minute hand would be pointing at a lie)

blocks.prompt: Circle the main idea of this passage.

answers: A clock keeps time by releasing stored energy in tiny equal steps, and a steady pendulum made those steps accurate

notes: Earth turns 15 degrees of longitude every hour

blocks.prompt: The Clock That Found the Sea
blocks.text: For most of history, a ship's captain could tell you how far north or south he was to within a mile, and had almost no idea how far east or west. Latitude is easy. Measure how high the sun climbs at noon, or how high the North Star sits above the horizon, and the sky hands you the answer. Longitude hides. Nothing in the sky points east. There was one way to catch it. The Earth turns once in twenty four hours, which works out to fifteen degrees of longitude every hour. If a sailor knew the exact time back at his home port and compared it to local noon on his ship, the gap between the two times would tell him his longitude. Three hours behind home meant forty five degrees west. The method is simple. The clock was the problem. Pendulum clocks were useless at sea. A pendulum needs to hang still, and a ship never is. Salt air rusted steel. Heat stretched the metal parts and cold shrank them, so a clock ran fast in one ocean and slow in the next. Ships wrecked for want of a clock. In 1707 four British warships ran onto the rocks near the Scilly Isles and around fourteen hundred sailors drowned. Seven years later, Parliament offered a fortune, up to twenty thousand pounds, to anyone who could solve longitude. John Harrison was a village carpenter who taught himself clockmaking. Most experts assumed the answer would come from astronomers reading the position of the moon. Harrison spent forty years proving the answer was a machine. He threw out the pendulum and used balance springs that did not care about rolling. He built parts from two different metals joined together, so that when heat stretched one, the pair bent back into shape and canceled its own error. He invented bearings that needed no oil, because oil thickened in the cold. His fourth attempt, H4, looked like an oversized pocket watch. In 1761 it sailed to Jamaica and back. Over eighty one days at sea, it lost about five seconds. The board holding the prize did not want to believe a carpenter, so it made him prove it again, then argued for years over the money. Harrison was seventy nine before the King stepped in and Parliament paid him most of what he was owed. By then his idea was already at sea in other men's ships.

6.title: The Clock That Started as a Shadow
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Clock That Started as a Shadow

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Quartz is piezoelectric: squeeze it, it makes voltage
Watch crystals vibrate 32,768 times a second
First quartz clock: Bell Labs, 1927
Since 1967 the second is defined by cesium-133
9,192,631,770 oscillations make one second
GPS satellites carry atomic clocks
Raise a clock a foot and it ticks faster

blocks.prompt: The Second Nobody Owns
blocks.text: For thousands of years, the Earth was the clock. A day was one turn of the planet, and every timepiece humans built was really just a machine trying to copy that turn. Divide a day by twenty four, then by sixty, then by sixty again, and you have a second. The definition was circular, but it worked, because nothing people made was accurate enough to catch the Earth out. Then, in 1927, two engineers at Bell Laboratories, Warren Marrison and J. W. Horton, built a clock around a sliver of quartz. Quartz has a strange property, discovered by the brothers Jacques and Pierre Curie in 1880. Squeeze the crystal and it produces a small voltage. Feed it a voltage and it flexes. Cut a piece of quartz to the right shape and it will vibrate at a rate it insists on, thousands of times a second, and hold that rate stubbornly. A modern watch crystal is tuned to vibrate 32,768 times per second, which is two multiplied by itself fifteen times. That number is not decoration. A simple circuit can halve a count, so halving fifteen times turns a blur of vibration into exactly one pulse per second. Quartz clocks were so steady that within a few years they caught the Earth out. The planet, it turned out, does not turn at a constant rate. It wobbles with the seasons, drags against the tides, and slows by a couple of thousandths of a second per century. The clock humanity had trusted for all of history was the sloppy one. So the second was taken away from the Earth and given to an atom. Since 1967, one second has been defined as the time it takes a cesium-133 atom to oscillate 9,192,631,770 times between two energy states. Nobody chose that number for its beauty. It was chosen to match the old astronomical second as closely as possible, so that nothing already built would have to be re-timed. An atom makes a better standard than a planet for one reason: every cesium atom in the universe is identical to every other one, and none of them wobble, wear out, or slow down. There is no master atom locked in a vault in Paris. Any laboratory anywhere can grow the second from scratch. The accuracy is hard to feel. The best atomic clocks running today would not gain or lose a second over the age of the universe. That sounds like showing off until you use it. Every satellite in the GPS system carries atomic clocks, and your phone finds itself by comparing how long each satellite's signal took to arrive. Radio waves travel about thirty centimeters in a billionth of a second, so a clock error of a few billionths puts you on the wrong street. Those satellite clocks also have to be corrected for relativity. They move fast, which slows their clocks down, and they orbit high above the Earth where gravity is weaker, which speeds them up. The two effects do not cancel. Left uncorrected, GPS would drift about ten kilometers off in a single day. Clocks have now become so sensitive that they work as instruments for measuring other things entirely. Raise an atomic clock by a foot and it ticks measurably faster, because gravity is a shade weaker up there. That is not a fault in the clock. It is the shape of time itself, showing up on a laboratory bench, in a device descended from a stick casting a shadow in Egyptian dirt.
